claim: A single Dcp1–Dcp2 decapping enzyme targets diverse classes of yeast mRNAs for decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay.
source: A single Dcp1–Dcp2 decapping enzyme targets diverse classes of yeast mRNAs for decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay, but the molecular mechanisms controlling mRNA selectivity by the enzyme remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes the context of the study.

claim: Dcp2 C-terminal domain cis-regulatory elements control decapping enzyme target specificity by orchestrating formation of distinct decapping complexes.
source: Through extensive genetic analyses we reveal that Dcp2 C-terminal domain cis-regulatory elements control decapping enzyme target specificity by orchestrating formation of distinct decapping complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the genetic analyses described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two Upf1-binding motifs direct the decapping enzyme to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay substrates.
source: Two Upf1-binding motifs direct the decapping enzyme to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay substrates, a single Edc3-binding motif targets both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates, and Pat1-binding leucine-rich motifs target Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates under selective conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: A single Edc3-binding motif targets both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
source: Two Upf1-binding motifs direct the decapping enzyme to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay substrates, a single Edc3-binding motif targets both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates, and Pat1-binding leucine-rich motifs target Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates under selective conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Pat1-binding leucine-rich motifs target Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates under selective conditions.
source: Two Upf1-binding motifs direct the decapping enzyme to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay substrates, a single Edc3-binding motif targets both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates, and Pat1-binding leucine-rich motifs target Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates under selective conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Edc3 is a common component of multiple decapping complexes.
source: Although it functions as a unique targeting component of specific complexes, Edc3 is a common component of multiple complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by two-hybrid data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Scd6 has specific binding sites on Dcp2.
source: Scd6 and Xrn1 also have specific binding sites on Dcp2, allowing them to be directly recruited to decapping complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Xrn1 has specific binding sites on Dcp2.
source: Scd6 and Xrn1 also have specific binding sites on Dcp2, allowing them to be directly recruited to decapping complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Upf1, Edc3, Scd6, and Pat1 function as regulatory subunits of the holo-decapping enzyme.
source: Collectively, our results demonstrate that Upf1, Edc3, Scd6, and Pat1 function as regulatory subunits of the holo-decapping enzyme, controlling both its substrate specificity and enzymatic activation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: Decapping plays a key role in general 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay.
source: Decapping plays a key role in general 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay (Decker and Parker, 1993), nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (He and Jacobson, 2001), AU-rich element-mediated mRNA decay (Fenger-Grøn et al., 2005; Pedro-Segura et al., 2008), microRNA-mediated gene silencing (Behm-Ansmant et al., 2006; Rehwinkel et al., 2005), and transcript-specific degradation (Badis et al., 2004; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Decapping plays a key role in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
source: Decapping plays a key role in general 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay (Decker and Parker, 1993), nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (He and Jacobson, 2001), AU-rich element-mediated mRNA decay (Fenger-Grøn et al., 2005; Pedro-Segura et al., 2008), microRNA-mediated gene silencing (Behm-Ansmant et al., 2006; Rehwinkel et al., 2005), and transcript-specific degradation (Badis et al., 2004; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, mRNA decapping is carried out by a single enzyme comprised of the Dcp1 regulatory subunit and the Dcp2 catalytic subunit.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, mRNA decapping is carried out by a single enzyme comprised of the Dcp1 regulatory subunit and the Dcp2 catalytic subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the yeast decapping enzyme.

claim: Dcp1 is a small EVH domain protein.
source: Dcp1 is a small EVH domain protein (Beelman et al., 1996; She et al., 2004) and Dcp2 is a 970-amino acid protein containing a highly conserved catalytic domain at its N-terminus and a largely disordered C-terminal domain embedded with multiple regulatory elements (Charenton et al., 2017; Dunckley and Parker, 1999; Gaudon et al., 1999; He and Jacobson, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dcp2 is a 970-amino acid protein containing a highly conserved catalytic domain at its N-terminus and a largely disordered C-terminal domain embedded with multiple regulatory elements.
source: Dcp1 is a small EVH domain protein (Beelman et al., 1996; She et al., 2004) and Dcp2 is a 970-amino acid protein containing a highly conserved catalytic domain at its N-terminus and a largely disordered C-terminal domain embedded with multiple regulatory elements (Charenton et al., 2017; Dunckley and Parker, 1999; Gaudon et al., 1999; He and Jacobson, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upf1 is required for degradation of nonsense-containing mRNAs.
source: Upf1 is required for degradation of nonsense-containing mRNAs (He and Jacobson, 2001; He et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 each target a specific subset of yeast mRNAs.
source: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 were originally thought to be required for general mRNA decay (Bouveret et al., 2000; Coller et al., 2001; Fischer and Weis, 2002; Hatfield et al., 1996; Tharun et al., 2000), but recent evidence indicates that they each target a specific subset of yeast mRNAs (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Scd6 targets a limited number of specific transcripts for decapping.
source: Scd6 targets a limited number of specific transcripts for decapping (Zeidan et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Edc3 exhibits exquisite substrate specificity and appears to target just two transcripts, YRA1 pre-mRNA and RPS28B mRNA.
source: Edc3 was also originally thought to be required for general mRNA decapping (Kshirsagar and Parker, 2004), but this factor exhibits exquisite substrate specificity and appears to target just two transcripts, YRA1 pre-mRNA and RPS28B mRNA (Badis et al., 2004; Dong et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of both Upf1-binding motifs eliminates Upf1's binding to Dcp2.
source: Deletion of either the first (U1D1) or the second (U1D2) Upf1-binding motif had no discernible effect on Upf1's binding to Dcp2, but loss of both Upf1-binding motifs (U1D1–U1D2) eliminated Upf1 binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of both Upf1-binding motifs does not affect Edc3 or Pat1 binding to Dcp2.
source: In contrast, loss of both Upf1-binding motifs affected neither Edc3 nor Pat1 binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The two Upf1-binding motifs have redundant functions and either can promote independent Upf1 binding to Dcp2.
source: These results indicate that the two Upf1-binding motifs have redundant functions and either can promote independent Upf1 binding to Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that deletion of either motif alone does not affect Upf1 binding, but deletion of both eliminates it.

claim: Loss of both Upf1-binding motifs caused approximately two- to threefold increases in the levels of NMD substrates.
source: However, loss of both Upf1-binding motifs caused approximately two- to threefold increases in the levels of these transcripts (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, HA-dcp2 alleles containing U1D1–U1D2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1C and supplements.

claim: Loss of UPF1 led to >10-fold increases for NMD substrates.
source: These increases were much smaller in magnitude than those caused by deletion of UPF1, which usually led to >10-fold increases for these transcripts.
evidence: This is a comparison of the effects of Upf1-binding motif deletion versus UPF1 gene deletion on NMD substrate levels.

claim: Loss of both Upf1-binding motifs did not affect the levels of the Edc3, Dhh1, Pat1/Lsm1, and Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates.
source: Loss of both Upf1-binding motifs did not affect the levels of the Edc3, Dhh1, Pat1/Lsm1, and Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data showing selective effects on NMD substrates.

claim: The two Upf1-binding motifs control targeting of the decapping enzyme to NMD substrates.
source: This selective stabilization of nonsense-containing mRNAs indicates that the two Upf1-binding motifs control targeting of the decapping enzyme to NMD substrates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the selective effects of Upf1-binding motif deletion on NMD substrates.

claim: The two Upf1-binding motifs have independent activities and are functionally redundant in promoting NMD.
source: In addition, the two motifs have independent activities and are functionally redundant in promoting NMD.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that deletion of either motif alone has no effect, but deletion of both has an effect.

claim: Decapping is not a major rate-limiting step in the overall NMD pathway.
source: The partial stabilization of NMD substrates caused by loss of both Upf1-binding motifs suggests that decapping is not a major rate-limiting step in the overall NMD pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that loss of Upf1-binding motifs causes only partial stabilization compared to UPF1 deletion.

claim: NMD substrates can be degraded by an alternative route in the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme by Upf1.
source: It also appears that NMD substrates can be degraded by an alternative route in the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme by Upf1.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the partial stabilization of NMD substrates when Upf1-binding motifs are deleted.

claim: Loss of E3 eliminates Edc3 binding to Dcp2.
source: Loss of E3 (E3D) did not affect the binding of Upf1 or Pat1 to Dcp2 but eliminated Edc3 binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B), indicating that the E3 motif promotes selective binding of Edc3 to the decapping enzyme.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The E3 motif promotes selective binding of Edc3 to the decapping enzyme.
source: Loss of E3 (E3D) did not affect the binding of Upf1 or Pat1 to Dcp2 but eliminated Edc3 binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B), indicating that the E3 motif promotes selective binding of Edc3 to the decapping enzyme.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing selective loss of Edc3 binding when E3 is deleted.

claim: Loss of the E3 motif caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA.
source: Compared to their fold increases in edc3Δ cells, loss of the Edc3-binding motif caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA (~twofold increases in both E3D and edc3Δ cells), but only partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA (threefold increase in E3D vs. ninefold increase in edc3Δ cells).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data comparing E3D and edc3Δ effects.

claim: Loss of the E3 motif caused only partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA.
source: Compared to their fold increases in edc3Δ cells, loss of the Edc3-binding motif caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA (~twofold increases in both E3D and edc3Δ cells), but only partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA (threefold increase in E3D vs. ninefold increase in edc3Δ cells).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data comparing E3D and edc3Δ effects.

claim: Deletion of EDC3 did not affect the levels of Dhh1 substrates.
source: Although deletion of EDC3 did not affect the levels of Dhh1 substrates, loss of the E3 motif caused partial stabilization of these mRNAs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, compare edc3Δ vs. HA-dcp2-E3D; He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of the E3 motif caused partial stabilization of Dhh1 substrates.
source: Although deletion of EDC3 did not affect the levels of Dhh1 substrates, loss of the E3 motif caused partial stabilization of these mRNAs (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, compare edc3Δ vs. HA-dcp2-E3D; He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: E3 controls targeting of the decapping enzyme to Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
source: This result indicates that, in addition to Edc3 substrates, E3 also controls targeting of the decapping enzyme to Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that E3 deletion affects Dhh1 substrates while EDC3 deletion does not.

claim: At least one additional factor may bind E3 and target the decapping enzyme to Dhh1-regulated mRNAs in the absence of Edc3.
source: Given the disparate mRNA decay phenotypes caused by edc3Δ and E3D for Dhh1 substrates, the E3-mediated targeting the decapping enzyme to Dhh1 substrates is unlikely to be carried out solely via interaction with Edc3. At least in the absence of Edc3, one additional factor may bind E3 (see below for Scd6 data) and target the decapping enzyme to Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different phenotypes of edc3Δ and E3D for Dhh1 substrates.

claim: Loss of E3-1 eliminates Edc3's binding to Dcp2.
source: Loss of E3-2 did not affect Edc3 binding to Dcp2, but loss of E3-1 eliminated Edc3's binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B), indicating that Edc3 binds to the conserved 17-amino acid segment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Edc3 binds to the conserved 17-amino acid segment E3-1.
source: Loss of E3-2 did not affect Edc3 binding to Dcp2, but loss of E3-1 eliminated Edc3's binding to Dcp2 (Figure 1B), indicating that Edc3 binds to the conserved 17-amino acid segment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that E3-1 but not E3-2 is required for Edc3 binding.

claim: Loss of E3-1 caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA and partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
source: Loss of E3-1 also caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA and partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the E3-1 element controls selective targeting of the decapping enzyme to both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The E3-1 element controls selective targeting of the decapping enzyme to both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
source: Loss of E3-1 also caused complete stabilization of RPS28B mRNA and partial stabilization of YRA1 pre-mRNA and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the E3-1 element controls selective targeting of the decapping enzyme to both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the northern blot data showing effects of E3-1 deletion on Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.

claim: Loss of the first five leucine-rich motifs (L1–L5) eliminated Pat1 interaction with Dcp2.
source: WT Dcp2 exhibited strong two-hybrid interaction with Pat1 and loss of the first five leucine-rich motifs (L1–L5) eliminated this interaction (Figure 2A, alleles LD1-5 to LD1-9).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of the last four leucine-rich motifs (L9–L6) did not affect Pat1 binding to Dcp2.
source: In contrast, loss of the last four leucine-rich motifs (L9–L6) did not affect Pat1 binding to Dcp2 (Figure 2A, allele L9-6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Leucine-rich motifs L1–L5 control the selective binding of Pat1 to Dcp2.
source: These results indicate that in the context of full-length Dcp2, leucine-rich motifs L1–L5 control the selective binding of Pat1 to Dcp2, most likely with a contribution from each motif.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing graded responses to deletion of different leucine-rich motifs.

claim: None of the leucine-rich element deletions altered the levels of Pat1-regulated mRNAs.
source: Surprisingly, none of the leucine-rich element deletions altered the levels of Pat1-regulated mRNAs, including both Pat1/Lsm1 and Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 2B, C.

claim: Pat1-mediated targeting of the decapping enzyme does not make a significant contribution to the overall decay of Pat1-regulated transcripts.
source: This indicates that Pat1-mediated targeting of the decapping enzyme does not make a significant contribution to the overall decay of Pat1-regulated transcripts, raising a question about the role of Pat1 in decapping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that leucine-rich motif deletions do not affect Pat1-regulated mRNA levels.

claim: Decapping is not rate limiting for Pat1-regulated mRNAs.
source: Because loss of Pat1 causes significant stabilization of both the Pat1/Lsm1 and Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates (Figure 2B; He et al., 2018), one possible explanation for this surprising observation is that decapping is not rate limiting for Pat1-regulated mRNAs, and Pat1 performs an unidentified major function upstream, independent of its role in the recruitment and activation of the decapping enzyme (Lobel et al., 2019; Nissan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the discrepancy between the effects of Pat1 deletion and leucine-rich motif deletion.

claim: In the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme, NMD substrates are still degraded by decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay.
source: In dcp2-U1D1-U1D2 cells, deletion of SKI2 or SKI7 did not cause additional stabilization of the NMD substrates (CYH2 pre-mRNA and can1-100 mRNA) whereas deletion of XRN1 caused substantial stabilization of these transcripts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3B, demonstrating that NMD substrates require Xrn1 but not the exosome for decay when Upf1-binding motifs are deleted.

claim: In the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme, Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates are still degraded by decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay.
source: Similarly, deletion of SKI2 or SKI7 did not cause additional stabilization of both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates, for example, YRA1 pre-mRNA, EDC1, and SDS23 mRNAs, in dcp2-E3D or E3D1 cells, but deletion of XRN1 caused substantial stabilization of each of these transcripts (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3B, demonstrating that Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates require Xrn1 but not the exosome for decay when the Edc3-binding motif is deleted.

claim: In the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme, Pat1/Lsm1 substrates are still degraded by decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay.
source: Deletions of SKI2 or SKI7 also did not cause discernible stabilization of the Pat1/Lsm1 substrates, BUR6, DIF1, and LSM3 mRNAs, in dcp2-LD1-9 cells, but deletion of XRN1 stabilized these mRNAs substantially (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3C, demonstrating that Pat1/Lsm1 substrates require Xrn1 but not the exosome for decay when Pat1-binding motifs are deleted.

claim: Decapping substrates can all be decapped by an alternative route when the normal Dcp2 cis-element-mediated active recruitment of the decapping enzyme is blocked.
source: These results indicate that, in the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme, the decapping substrates examined here, including the NMD, Edc3, Dhh1, and Pat1/Lsm1 substrates, are not degraded by exosome-dependent 3′ to 5′ decay, but are all still degraded by decapping-dependent 5′ to 3′ decay. Hence, these decapping substrates can all be decapped by an alternative route when the normal Dcp2 cis-element-mediated active recruitment of the decapping enzyme is blocked.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that deletion of XRN1 but not SKI2 or SKI7 causes additional stabilization in Dcp2 cis-element mutants.

claim: Combining the leucine-rich element deletions with the Edc3-binding element deletions caused additional substantial stabilization of the Edc3 substrate YRA1 pre-mRNA and the Dhh1 substrates.
source: Although none of the leucine-rich element deletions affected the decay of Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates (Figure 2B), combining the leucine-rich element deletions LD1-8, LD1-9, LD9-3, and LD9-2 with the Edc3-binding element deletions E3D or E3D1 caused additional substantial stabilization of the Edc3 substrate YRA1 pre-mRNA and the Dhh1 substrates EDC1, SDS23, and HXT6 mRNAs (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 4B, demonstrating synergistic effects of deleting both Edc3- and Pat1-binding motifs.

claim: In the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme by Edc3, both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates are degraded by the Pat1-mediated decay pathway.
source: These results indicate that in the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme by Edc3, both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates are degraded by the Pat1-mediated decay pathway, suggesting that Pat1-mediated decapping serves as a backup or fail-safe system in the decay of Edc3 and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the synergistic effects of deleting both Edc3- and Pat1-binding motifs on Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.

claim: Pat1-mediated decapping serves as a backup or fail-safe system in the decay of Edc3 and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
source: These results indicate that in the absence of active recruitment of the decapping enzyme by Edc3, both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates are degraded by the Pat1-mediated decay pathway, suggesting that Pat1-mediated decapping serves as a backup or fail-safe system in the decay of Edc3 and Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Pat1-binding motifs only affect Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates when the Edc3-binding motif is also deleted.

claim: Combining the leucine-rich element deletion LD1-9 with the Upf1-binding element deletion U1D1–U1D2 did not cause additional stabilization of the NMD substrates.
source: Combining the leucine-rich element deletion LD1-9 with the Upf1-binding element deletion U1D1–U1D2 did not cause additional stabilization of the NMD substrates CYH2 pre-mRNA, can1-100, and ade2-1 mRNAs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, allele U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 compared to allele U1D1-U1D2 in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 4C, indicating that Pat1-mediated decapping does not serve as a backup for NMD.

claim: Pat1-mediated decapping either does not function as a backup system or does not make a significant contribution to the decay of NMD substrates in the absence of Upf1-mediated recruitment of the decapping enzyme.
source: These results indicate that Pat1-mediated decapping either does not function as a backup system or does not make a significant contribution to the decay of NMD substrates in the absence of Upf1-mediated recruitment of the decapping enzyme.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that combining Upf1- and Pat1-binding motif deletions does not cause additional stabilization of NMD substrates.

claim: Edc3-mediated decapping may function as a backup system for some nonsense-containing mRNAs.
source: Further combining the Edc3-binding motif deletions E3D or E3D1 also did not cause additional stabilization of the CYH2 pre-mRNA and can1-100 mRNA, but did appear to cause small but significant increases in ade2-1 mRNA levels (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, compare allele U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 to alleles E3D-U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 and E3D1-U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9). These results indicate that Pat1-mediated decapping either does not function as a backup system or does not make a significant contribution to the decay of NMD substrates in the absence of Upf1-mediated recruitment of the decapping enzyme. However, Edc3-mediated decapping may function as a backup system for some nonsense-containing mRNAs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the small but significant effect of adding Edc3-binding motif deletion to Upf1- and Pat1-binding motif deletions for ade2-1 mRNA.

claim: Eliminating all the known-binding motifs in the Dcp2 C-terminal domain did not have any significant effect on the levels of accumulation of the Pat1/Lsm1 substrates.
source: Further, the combination of element deletions E3D-U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 eliminates all the binding motifs of known decapping activators in Dcp2, yet this combination of deletions still did not have any significant effect on the levels of accumulation of the Pat1/Lsm1 substrates (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neither Edc3-mediated decapping nor Upf1-mediated decapping functions as a backup system in decay of Pat1/Lsm1 substrates.
source: This result indicates that neither Edc3-mediated decapping nor Upf1-mediated decapping functions as a backup system in decay of Pat1/Lsm1 substrates, raising the possibility that Pat1/Lsm1 substrates can be decapped without the enhancement function of any decapping activators.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that eliminating all known binding motifs does not affect Pat1/Lsm1 substrates.

claim: The Edc3-binding motif can function independently of other elements and promote specific mRNA decay activities.
source: The combination of element deletions U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 created a dcp2 allele harboring a lonely Edc3-binding motif. This dcp2 allele had the activity of WT DCP2 in promoting the decay of both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, compare U1D1-U1D2-LD1-9 to WT).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data showing that the Edc3-binding motif alone is sufficient for decay of Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.

claim: Each of the Upf1-binding motifs can function independently of other elements and promote specific mRNA decay activities.
source: Similarly, the combination of deletions E3D-U1D2-LD1-9 and E3D1-U1D2-LD1-9 created two dcp2 alleles harboring a lonely Upf1-binding motif U11, and the combination of deletions E3D-U1D1-LD1-9 and E3D1-U1D1-LD1-9 created two dcp2 alleles harboring a lonely Upf1-binding motif U12. Each of these four dcp2 alleles had the activity of WT DCP2 in promoting NMD (Figure 4C, compare alleles E3D-U1D2-LD1-9, E3D1-U1D2-LD1-9, E3D-U1D1-LD1-9, and E3D1-U1D1-LD1-9 to WT).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data showing that either Upf1-binding motif alone is sufficient for NMD.

claim: Deletion of EDC3 caused additional seven- to eightfold stabilization of the Edc3 substrate YRA1 pre-mRNA in E3D or E3D1 cells.
source: Deletion of EDC3 caused additional seven- to eightfold stabilization of the Edc3 substrate YRA1 pre-mRNA in E3D or E3D1 cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 4D, demonstrating that Edc3 has functions beyond recruiting the decapping enzyme.

claim: Deletion of EDC3 caused additional stabilization of the Dhh1 substrates EDC1 and SDS23 mRNAs and the Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates HSP12 and HXT6 mRNAs in E3D or E3D1 cells.
source: Deletion of EDC3 also caused additional stabilization of the Dhh1 substrates EDC1 and SDS23 mRNAs and the Pat1/Lsm1/Dhh1 substrates HSP12 and HXT6 mRNAs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Edc3 is directly involved in the decay of Dhh1-regulated mRNAs.
source: These results provide evidence that Edc3 is directly involved in the decay of Dhh1-regulated mRNAs, and demonstrate that besides recruiting the decapping enzyme, Edc3 indeed carries out an additional function in decay of both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that EDC3 deletion causes additional stabilization in E3D cells.

claim: Besides recruiting the decapping enzyme, Edc3 carries out an additional function in decay of both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
source: These results provide evidence that Edc3 is directly involved in the decay of Dhh1-regulated mRNAs, and demonstrate that besides recruiting the decapping enzyme, Edc3 indeed carries out an additional function in decay of both Edc3 and Dhh1 substrates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that EDC3 deletion causes additional stabilization beyond what is caused by E3D deletion.

claim: The Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction requires both the Dcp2 C-terminal domain and Edc3.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, Dhh1 exhibited strong two-hybrid interaction with Dcp1 in WT cells. Deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 did not affect the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction. In contrast, loss of the entire C-terminal domain of Dcp2 or deletion of EDC3 eliminated Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction. These results indicate that the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction observed in WT cells requires both the Dcp2 C-terminal domain and Edc3, suggesting that this interaction occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5A, demonstrating factor requirements for the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction.

claim: The Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 complex.
source: These results indicate that the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction observed in WT cells requires both the Dcp2 C-terminal domain and Edc3, suggesting that this interaction occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction requires Dcp2 C-terminal domain and Edc3.

claim: The Dcp2 Edc3-binding motif promotes assembly of the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 decapping complex in vivo.
source: Further, in a WT EDC3 background, Dcp2 C-terminal truncations maintaining the E3 motif left the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction intact. In contrast, the Dcp2 C-terminal truncation eliminating the E3 motif abolished the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5B). These results show that the observed Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction also requires an intact Dcp2 E3 motif, indicating that the Dcp2 Edc3-binding motif promotes assembly of the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 decapping complex in vivo (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that the E3 motif is required for the Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction.

claim: Dhh1 assembles into the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 via association with Edc3.
source: In an edc3Δ background, Dhh1 exhibited no interaction with Dcp1 (the slight blue color of the transformants was due to self-activation of Gal4(DB)-Dhh1 fusion protein) (Figure 5B; He and Jacobson, 2015), indicating that Dhh1 assembles into the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Dhh1 via association with Edc3, consistent with the physical interaction between these two factors (He and Jacobson, 2015; Sharif et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Dhh1:Dcp1 interaction is lost in edc3Δ cells, supported by citations to previous work showing Dhh1-Edc3 interaction.

claim: Upf1:Dcp1 interaction in WT cells requires the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and is enhanced by the presence of Edc3.
source: In WT cells, Upf1 also exhibited strong two-hybrid interaction with Dcp1 (Figure 5A). Deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 did not affect Upf1:Dcp1 interaction. In contrast, deletion of EDC3 diminished and loss of the entire C-terminal domain of Dcp2 eliminated Upf1:Dcp1 interaction. These results indicate that Upf1:Dcp1 interaction in WT cells requires the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and is enhanced by the presence of Edc3, suggesting that this interaction occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Upf1-binding motifs U11 and U12 can both promote the assembly of Upf1-containing decapping complexes.
source: In a WT EDC3 background, Dcp2 C-terminal truncations eliminating the second Upf1-binding motif U12 did not affect Upf1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5B, alleles N630 and N475); however, further eliminating the first Upf1-binding motif U11 abolished Upf1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5B, alleles N400, N300, and N245). In an edc3Δ background, Upf1 interacted weakly with Dcp1 and Dcp2 C-terminal truncations eliminating the second Upf1-binding motif U12 abolished Upf1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5B, compare alleles N771 to N630). These results indicate that the Upf1-binding motifs U11 and U12 can both promote the assembly of Upf1-containing decapping complexes and that Edc3 enhances the binding of Upf1 to the U11 motif to promote assembly of the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 decapping complex in vivo (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing differential requirements for U11 and U12 in EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds.

claim: Edc3 enhances the binding of Upf1 to the U11 motif to promote assembly of the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 decapping complex in vivo.
source: These results indicate that the Upf1-binding motifs U11 and U12 can both promote the assembly of Upf1-containing decapping complexes and that Edc3 enhances the binding of Upf1 to the U11 motif to promote assembly of the Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 decapping complex in vivo (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Edc3 affects the requirement for specific Upf1-binding motifs.

claim: Pat1 can associate with the Dcp1–Dcp2 decapping enzyme both in the presence and absence of Edc3.
source: In contrast to Dhh1 and Upf1, Pat1 exhibited only weak two-hybrid interaction with Dcp1 in WT cells (Figure 5A). Deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 did not alter Pat1:Dcp1 interaction, but loss of the entire Dcp2 C-terminal domain eliminated Pat1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5A). Interestingly, deletion of EDC3 enhanced Pat1:Dcp1 interaction (Figure 5A). These results indicate that Pat1 can associate with the Dcp1–Dcp2 decapping enzyme both in the presence and absence of Edc3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Pat1:Dcp1 interaction occurs in both EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds.

claim: Pat1:Dcp1 interaction requires the L1 motif in Dcp2 regardless of the cellular status of Edc3.
source: Eliminating different leucine-rich motifs between L2 and L9 by progressive Dcp2 C-terminal truncations did not significantly alter the respective Pat1:Dcp1 interaction strength in EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds. However, further eliminating the leucine-rich motif L1 abolished Pat1:Dcp1 interaction in an EDC3 background and greatly diminished Pat1:Dcp1 interaction in an edc3Δ background (Figure 5B). These results show that Pat1:Dcp1 interaction requires the L1 motif in Dcp2 regardless of the cellular status of Edc3, suggesting that this motif may promote assembly of several different decapping complexes including a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Pat1 complex (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that L1 is required for Pat1:Dcp1 interaction in both EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds.

claim: Dcp2 bridges an interaction between Upf1 and Edc3.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, in contrast to the Upf1:Dcp1 interaction, Upf1 did not show two-hybrid interaction with Edc3 in WT cells. Upf1 also did not show interaction with Edc3 in upf1Δ, pat1Δ, or scd6Δ cells. Surprisingly, Upf1 exhibited strong two-hybrid interaction with Edc3 in edc3Δ cells. Deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 in edc3Δ cells did not alter this strong Upf1:Edc3 interaction; however, deletion of the entire Dcp2 C-terminal domain in edc3Δ cells eliminated Upf1:Edc3 interaction. These results indicate that Dcp2 bridges an interaction between Upf1 and Edc3 and that this bridged Upf1:Edc3 interaction is inhibited by endogenous Edc3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Upf1:Edc3 interaction requires Dcp2 C-terminal domain and is only observed in edc3Δ cells.

claim: The bridged Upf1:Edc3 interaction is inhibited by endogenous Edc3.
source: These results indicate that Dcp2 bridges an interaction between Upf1 and Edc3 and that this bridged Upf1:Edc3 interaction is inhibited by endogenous Edc3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Upf1:Edc3 interaction is only observed in edc3Δ cells.

claim: The U12 motif can promote assembly of a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 decapping complex in vivo, with Upf1 binding to the Dcp2 U12 motif.
source: In an edc3Δ background, eliminating the second Upf1-binding motif U12 in Dcp2 by C-terminal truncation abolished the Upf1:Edc3 interaction (Figure 5C, compare alleles N771 and N630). This result shows that the Upf1:Edc3 interaction requires the U12 motif in Dcp2 and that this motif can promote assembly of a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Upf1 decapping complex in vivo, with Upf1 binding to the Dcp2 U12 motif (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that U12 is required for the Upf1:Edc3 interaction in edc3Δ cells.

claim: Dcp2 bridges an interaction between Pat1 and Edc3.
source: Similar to the Upf1:Edc3 interaction, Pat1 also did not show two-hybrid interaction with Edc3 in WT cells, deletion of EDC3 promoted Pat1:Edc3 interaction, and deletion of the entire C-terminal domain of Dcp2 eliminated Pat1:Edc3 interaction in edc3Δ cells (Figure 5A). These results indicate that Dcp2 also bridges an interaction between Pat1 and Edc3 and that this bridged interaction is inhibited by endogenous Edc3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Pat1:Edc3 interaction requires Dcp2 C-terminal domain and is only observed in edc3Δ cells.

claim: The L2 motif can promote assembly of a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Pat1 decapping complex in vivo, with Pat1 binding to the Dcp2 L2 motif.
source: In an edc3Δ background, eliminating different leucine-rich motifs between L3 and L9 did not affect Pat1:Edc3 interaction; however, further eliminating the L2 motif abolished Pat1:Edc3 interaction (Figure 5C). This result shows that Pat1:Edc3 interaction requires the L2 motif in Dcp2 and that this motif can promote assembly of a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Pat1 decapping complex in vivo, with Pat1 binding to the Dcp2 L2 motif (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that L2 is required for the Pat1:Edc3 interaction in edc3Δ cells.

claim: Endogenous Edc3 can completely inhibit the bridged molecular interactions between Edc3 and Upf1 or Pat1.
source: Our observation that endogenous Edc3 can completely inhibit the bridged molecular interactions between Edc3 and Upf1 or Pat1 is intriguing (Figure 5A). It indicates that free Edc3-binding sites from Dcp2 molecules are limiting and suggests that the entire pool of Dcp2 molecules are likely to be stably bound by endogenous Edc3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Upf1:Edc3 and Pat1:Edc3 interactions are only observed in edc3Δ cells.

claim: The entire pool of Dcp2 molecules are likely to be stably bound by endogenous Edc3.
source: It indicates that free Edc3-binding sites from Dcp2 molecules are limiting and suggests that the entire pool of Dcp2 molecules are likely to be stably bound by endogenous Edc3. Consistent with this interpretation, as demonstrated above, Edc3 exists as a common component of multiple decapping complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that endogenous Edc3 inhibits bridged interactions.

claim: Xrn1 interacted with Dcp1, Edc3, Pat1, and Upf1.
source: To assess potential coupling between decapping and 5′ to 3′ exoribonucleolytic decay, we tested two hybrid interactions between Xrn1 and all known decapping factors. Xrn1 interacted with Dcp1, Edc3, Pat1, and Upf1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Xrn1 did not interact with full-length Dcp2, but interacted with a 726-amino acid C-terminal Dcp2 fragment Dcp2-ND244.
source: Xrn1 did not interact with full-length Dcp2, but interacted with a 726-amino acid C-terminal Dcp2 fragment Dcp2-ND244 (Figure 6A), suggesting that Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 may be dependent on a specific Dcp2 conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 may be dependent on a specific Dcp2 conformation.
source: Xrn1 did not interact with full-length Dcp2, but interacted with a 726-amino acid C-terminal Dcp2 fragment Dcp2-ND244 (Figure 6A), suggesting that Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 may be dependent on a specific Dcp2 conformation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Xrn1 interacts with a Dcp2 fragment but not full-length Dcp2.

claim: Xrn1 may bind to Dcp2 and Pat1 directly.
source: Deletions of EDC3, UPF1, or PAT1 and elimination of the entire C-terminal domain of Dcp2 did not affect binding of Xrn1 to Dcp2-ND244 or Pat1 (Figure 6C), suggesting that Xrn1 may bind to Dcp2 and Pat1 directly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Xrn1:Dcp2-ND244 and Xrn1:Pat1 interactions are not affected by deletions of other factors.

claim: Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 required a large Dcp2 fragment with the minimal Xrn1-binding region encompassing an internal fragment from aa 316–575.
source: In contrast to the binding of Edc3, Upf1, and Pat1 to Dcp2, Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 required a large Dcp2 fragment with the minimal Xrn1-binding region encompassing an internal fragment from aa 316–575 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 6D and supplement.

claim: Xrn1:Dcp1 interaction is bridged by Dcp2 and enhanced by Edc3, and occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Xrn1 complex.
source: In contrast to the Xrn1:Dcp2-ND244 and Xrn1:Pat1 interactions, the Xrn1:Dcp1, Xrn1:Edc3, and Xrn1:Upf1 interactions are all bridged by Dcp2. As shown in Figure 6B, deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 did not significantly affect Xrn1:Dcp1 interaction. However, elimination of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain or deletion of EDC3 abolished Xrn1:Dcp1 interaction, suggesting that Xrn1:Dcp1 interaction is bridged by Dcp2 and enhanced by Edc3, and occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Xrn1 complex (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing factor requirements for the Xrn1:Dcp1 interaction.

claim: Xrn1:Edc3 interaction is bridged by Dcp2.
source: Deletions of EDC3, UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6 did not affect Xrn1:Edc3 interaction, but elimination of the entire Dcp2 C-terminal domain abolished Xrn1:Edc3 interaction (Figure 6B), indicating that this interaction is bridged by Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Xrn1:Edc3 interaction requires Dcp2 C-terminal domain.

claim: Xrn1:Upf1 interaction is bridged by Dcp2 and occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Xrn1–Upf1 complex.
source: Elimination of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain and deletion of EDC3 both abolished Xrn1:Upf1 interaction (Figure 6B), indicating that this interaction is bridged by Dcp2 and occurs in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Xrn1–Upf1 complex (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing factor requirements for the Xrn1:Upf1 interaction.

claim: Xrn1 binds to an internal fragment of Dcp2 and is recruited to the decapping complex by Dcp2.
source: Collectively, our two-hybrid analyses show that Xrn1 binds to an internal fragment of Dcp2 and is recruited to the decapping complex by Dcp2.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the two-hybrid data showing Xrn1 binding to Dcp2 fragments and its interactions with other decapping factors.

claim: Two important events in 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay, Dcp2-mediated decapping and Xrn1-mediated 5′ to 3′ exoribonucleolytic digestion, are physically coupled in vivo.
source: These results indicate that two important events in 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay, Dcp2-mediated decapping and Xrn1-mediated 5′ to 3′ exoribonucleolytic digestion, are physically coupled in vivo, suggesting that in addition to controlling the selective targeting of the decapping enzyme to different decapping substrates, the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 also controls efficient 5′ to 3′ exonucleolytic decay, ensuring that decapped mRNAs are degraded in a timely manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that Xrn1 is recruited to decapping complexes by Dcp2.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Dcp2 controls efficient 5′ to 3′ exonucleolytic decay, ensuring that decapped mRNAs are degraded in a timely manner.
source: These results indicate that two important events in 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay, Dcp2-mediated decapping and Xrn1-mediated 5′ to 3′ exoribonucleolytic digestion, are physically coupled in vivo, suggesting that in addition to controlling the selective targeting of the decapping enzyme to different decapping substrates, the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 also controls efficient 5′ to 3′ exonucleolytic decay, ensuring that decapped mRNAs are degraded in a timely manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that Xrn1 is recruited to decapping complexes by Dcp2.

claim: Scd6 interacted with Dcp1, Dcp2, Edc3, and Pat1.
source: We found that Scd6 interacted with Dcp1, Dcp2, Edc3, and Pat1, but did not interact with all other decay factors tested, including Dhh1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by two-hybrid data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The observed Scd6:Dcp1 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, Scd6 interacted with Dcp1 strongly in WT cells and this interaction was not affected by deletions of UPF1, PAT1, or SCD6. However, Scd6:Dcp1 interaction was greatly diminished by deletion of EDC3, and was eliminated by the dcp2-N245 truncation. In an edc3Δ background, Scd6 interacted weakly with Dcp1. This weak Scd6:Dcp1 interaction was not affected by deletions of UPF1 or SCD6, but was eliminated by deletion of PAT1 or the dcp2-N245 truncation. Together, these results indicate that the observed Scd6:Dcp1 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and that both Edc3 and Pat1 can promote the joining of Scd6 into decapping complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing factor requirements for the Scd6:Dcp1 interaction.

claim: Both Edc3 and Pat1 can promote the joining of Scd6 into decapping complexes.
source: Together, these results indicate that the observed Scd6:Dcp1 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and that both Edc3 and Pat1 can promote the joining of Scd6 into decapping complexes. In the presence of Edc3, Scd6 exists in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 complex and, in the absence of Edc3, Scd6 can exist in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing different factor requirements for Scd6:Dcp1 interaction in EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds.

claim: In the presence of Edc3, Scd6 exists in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 complex.
source: In the presence of Edc3, Scd6 exists in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 complex and, in the absence of Edc3, Scd6 can exist in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Scd6:Dcp1 interaction is enhanced by Edc3.

claim: In the absence of Edc3, Scd6 can exist in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complex.
source: In the presence of Edc3, Scd6 exists in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 complex and, in the absence of Edc3, Scd6 can exist in a Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Scd6:Dcp1 interaction requires Pat1 in edc3Δ background.

claim: The observed Scd6:Edc3 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2.
source: Scd6 interacted weakly with Edc3 in WT cells (Figure 7B). Much like the Upf1:Edc3 and Pat1:Edc3 interactions shown in Figure 5A, the Scd6:Edc3 interaction was enhanced by deletion of EDC3 and was eliminated by the dcp2-N245 truncation in both EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds (Figure 7B). These results indicate that the observed Scd6:Edc3 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and that endogenous Edc3 inhibits the Scd6:Edc3 two-hybrid interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Scd6:Edc3 interaction requires Dcp2 C-terminal domain.

claim: Endogenous Edc3 inhibits the Scd6:Edc3 two-hybrid interaction.
source: These results indicate that the observed Scd6:Edc3 interaction in WT cells is bridged by the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 and that endogenous Edc3 inhibits the Scd6:Edc3 two-hybrid interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that Scd6:Edc3 interaction is enhanced in edc3Δ cells.

claim: Pat1 may regulate the interaction of Scd6 with an Edc3-containing decapping complex.
source: Interestingly, in an EDC3 background, deletion of PAT1 also promoted the Scd6:Edc3 interaction (Figure 7B), suggesting that Pat1 may regulate the interaction of Scd6 with an Edc3-containing decapping complex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that PAT1 deletion enhances Scd6:Edc3 interaction in EDC3 background.

claim: The Scd6:Dcp2 and Scd6:Pat1 interactions appear to be direct.
source: The Scd6:Dcp2 and Scd6:Pat1 interactions observed in WT cells (Figure 7A) appear to be direct, as these two interactions were not affected by the dcp2-N245 truncation or the deletions of the EDC3 or PAT1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that Scd6:Dcp2 and Scd6:Pat1 interactions are not affected by deletions of other factors.

claim: Scd6 interacts with multiple decapping factors including Dcp1, Dcp2, Edc3, and Pat1.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Scd6 interacts with multiple decapping factors including Dcp1, Dcp2, Edc3, and Pat1 and that, depending on the Edc3 status in the cell, Scd6 can exist in Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 or Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complexes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the two-hybrid data showing Scd6 interactions with multiple factors.

claim: Depending on the Edc3 status in the cell, Scd6 can exist in Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 or Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complexes.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Scd6 interacts with multiple decapping factors including Dcp1, Dcp2, Edc3, and Pat1 and that, depending on the Edc3 status in the cell, Scd6 can exist in Dcp1–Dcp2–Edc3–Scd6 or Dcp1–Dcp2–Scd6–Pat1 complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing different Scd6 interactions in EDC3 and edc3Δ backgrounds.

claim: Scd6 most likely binds multiple elements in Dcp2.
source: The N101-300 and N246-300 fragments and the ND244 fragment share a 55-amino acid overlap of the Edc3-binding region. The six C-terminal fragments share different overlaps with the N244 fragment, but have no overlap with the two N-terminal fragments. Thus, the pattern of Scd6 binding to different Dcp2 fragments indicates that Scd6 most likely binds multiple elements in Dcp2 and that one of the Scd6-binding elements coincides with the Edc3-binding region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing Scd6 binding to multiple Dcp2 fragments.

claim: One of the Scd6-binding elements coincides with the Edc3-binding region.
source: Thus, the pattern of Scd6 binding to different Dcp2 fragments indicates that Scd6 most likely binds multiple elements in Dcp2 and that one of the Scd6-binding elements coincides with the Edc3-binding region.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing Scd6 binding to Dcp2 fragments that include the Edc3-binding region.

claim: The E3-1 and E3-2 motifs can both promote Scd6 binding and function redundantly to recruit Sdc6 to Dcp2.
source: Loss of the Edc3-binding motif E3-1 (E3D1) or the E3-2 motif (D3D2) partially weakened the Scd6:Dcp2 interaction; however, loss of both the E3-1 and E3-2 motifs (E3D) eliminated Scd6:Dcp2 interaction (Figure 7E, compare the E3D1 and E3D2 alleles to all the E3D-containing alleles). These results indicate that the E3-1 and E3-2 motifs can both promote Scd6 binding and function redundantly to recruit Sdc6 to Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that deletion of both E3-1 and E3-2 is required to eliminate Scd6:Dcp2 interaction.

claim: Leucine-rich motifs L3 and L5 are required for Scd6 binding to Dcp2.
source: Loss of the leucine-rich motifs L1 and L2 (LD1-2) did not affect the binding of Scd6 to Dcp2; further loss of the L3 motif (LD1-3) or both L3 and L4 motifs (LD1-4) partially weakened Scd6:Dcp2 interaction to similar extents, and further loss of the L5 motif (LD1-5) eliminated Scd6:Dcp2 interaction (Figure 7F). These results indicate that leucine-rich motifs L3 and L5 are required for Scd6 binding to Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing graded effects of deleting leucine-rich motifs on Scd6:Dcp2 interaction.

claim: Leucine-rich motifs L8 and L9 are required for Scd6 binding to Dcp2.
source: Interestingly, loss of the last leucine-rich motif L9 (LD9) also weakened Scd6:Dcp2 interaction, and loss of the last two leucine-rich motifs L8 and L9 (LD9-8) eliminated Scd6:Dcp2 interaction (Figure 7F), indicating that leucine-rich motifs L8 and L9 are also required for Scd6 binding to Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the two-hybrid data showing that deletion of L8 and L9 eliminates Scd6:Dcp2 interaction.

claim: Scd6 functions redundantly with Edc3 in targeting the decapping enzyme to Dhh1 substrates.
source: Since Scd6 also binds to the Edc3-binding motif E3-1 and exists in both Edc3 and Pat1-containing decapping complexes (Figure 7B, E), we propose that Scd6 functions redundantly with Edc3 in targeting the decapping enzyme to Dhh1 substrates.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that Scd6 binds to the Edc3-binding motif and the different phenotypes of edc3Δ and E3D for Dhh1 substrates.
